config.prompt: One cloud, two statements — drag the divider:

before.label: what the scatter records
before.text: r ≈ 0.95 — points hug the line; 0.8 more study hours predicted per extra exam point, inside the measured range

after.label: what it cannot show

statements.s: The explanatory variable belongs on the x-axis and the response on the y-axis.
statements.why: The convention follows the question: given x, predict y.

statements.s: Swapping the axes just rotates the same line.
statements.why: Least squares draws a genuinely different line — a different question gets a different answer.

statements.s: Either variable can be predicted from the other, and the two resulting lines differ.
statements.why: Which assignment you make should be picked by the question you intend to ask.

activities.anchor: one billionaire in an income study
activities.caption: one reading rule for r is wrong — click it
activities.name: crRSpot

config.prompt: One line of this r-reading guide is wrong — click it:
lines: r runs from −1 to +1: direction from the sign, straight-line strength from the magnitude.
Calibration: |r| above 0.8 strong, 0.5–0.8 moderate, 0.2–0.5 weak, below 0.2 negligible — and 'strong' is contextual.
r is dimensionless: heights in metres or inches give the same r.
r measures agreement: x and x + 10 correlate perfectly, so they agree perfectly.
A perfect U-shaped curve also scores r ≈ 0 — the coefficient only measures straight-line co-movement.
config.correction: r measures association, not agreement — x and x + 10 correlate perfectly while differing by 10 everywhere.
config.why: Anscombe's quartet shares r = 0.816 across a clean trend, a perfect curve, an outlier-distorted cloud and a vertical line — plot, always plot.

activities.anchor: honours the average behaviour of both
activities.caption: semi-averages, by hand — rebuild the worked line
activities.name: crSemiOrder

config.prompt: Eight students' (hours, score) pairs — order the method:
items: Order the data by x and split into a lower half and an upper half
Lower-half means: x̄₁ = 2.5, ȳ₁ = 52; upper-half means: x̄₂ = 6.5, ȳ₂ = 72
Line through the two mean points: gradient = (72 − 52) ÷ (6.5 − 2.5) = 5 marks per hour
Intercept: 52 = a + 5 × 2.5 gives a = 39.5, so y ≈ 39.5 + 5x
Least squares then refines it using every point — and always passes through (x̄, ȳ), the cloud's centre of gravity
config.why: Each half's mean is that half's balance point, so the line joining them summarises the trend with the noise averaged out.

config.text: The gradient is the %%0%%: about %%1%% extra marks per extra revision hour, on average, within the measured range. Predicting inside the observed x-range is %%2%% — supported by the data; predicting outside it is %%3%% — the pattern's continuation is unverified.
config.hint: One of the last two starts with 'inter-', the other with 'extra-'.

activities.caption: you hold a strong correlation — walk the claim
activities.name: crCausBranch

config.root: A strong correlation lands on your desk. Decide what you may claim.

start.text: Ice-cream sales correlate with drownings. The causal reading is:

choices.label: Ice-cream causes drowning
choices.feedback: Causal in neither direction — the same third variable drives both.

choices.label: A lurking third variable drives both
choices.feedback: Summer: hot days sell ice-cream and fill the water. r is blind to it.

lurk.text: Children's shoe size correlates with reading age. What is doing the work?

choices.label: Age — the lurking variable
choices.feedback: Older children have bigger feet and read better; age causes both.

choices.label: Big feet make reading easier
choices.feedback: No — the correlation rides on age, not feet.

licensed.text: Licensed 'because' claims need experiments, controlled variables or the causal-inference machinery of the expert tier.

silly.text: Dead end — the regression line reports how variables move together; the explanation belongs to experiments and controlled variables, and reverse causation is invisible to r.

config.why: Correlation is evidence of association — no more.

config.prompt: Revision hours and scores correlate at r = 0.9. What percentage of the score variation does the fitted line explain?
config.why: r² = 0.81 — while r = 0.5, which intuition calls moderate, is only r² = 0.25. 'X explains 30% of the variation in Y' is an r² in its practical clothes.
config.context: The page's own scatter: r ≈ 0.95, so r² ≈ 0.9 — that is what 'points hug the line' means numerically.
